query: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

generation.hypothesis: The use of density functional theory (DFT) calculations can effectively control phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) by predicting the formation energies and stability of constituent phases.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs with a disordered face-centered cubic (FCC) structure
generation.intervention: DFT calculations with a plane-wave basis set and the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange-correlation functional
generation.conditions: Calculations performed at 0 K with a 500 eV plane-wave cutoff energy
generation.structural_mediator: Formation energies and phase stability diagrams
generation.mechanism: Ab initio predictions of phase stability and transformation pathways
generation.predicted_outcome: A 20% reduction in the volume fraction of the B2 phase relative to the baseline, as measured by X-ray diffraction (XRD)
generation.baseline: As-cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs without DFT-guided phase control
generation.boundary: ±5% uncertainty in the predicted volume fraction
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty in the accuracy of DFT predictions for complex HEA systems, potential limitations in the transferability of DFT results to experimental conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Experimental synthesis and characterization of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs with and without DFT-guided phase control
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured volume fraction of the B2 phase in DFT-guided HEAs is not within 10% of the predicted value, the hypothesis is falsified

frame.limitation: lack of effective method for controlling phase evolution

families.principle: ab initio calculations or molecular dynamics simulations

families.best_lever: X-ray diffraction (XRD) or transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
